title: Digital wallet / payment service
scopeHtml:
Scope: wallets, idempotent transfers, ledger, ordered locking against deadlock, SQL transaction view.

Scope: wallets, idempotent transfers, ledger, ordered locking against deadlock, SQL transaction view.

notes.title: Requirements
notes.html:
Design a digital wallet and payment service: open wallets, transfer money between them, never lose or create money, and make retries safe.

Clarify:

  • Functional: create wallet with balance, transfer A to B, record every transaction (success or failure), query balance.
  • Rules: no negative balances; amount must be positive; the same request sent twice (network retry) must charge once.
  • Out of scope: bank top-up, KYC, currency conversion, fraud scoring.
  • Scale talk: Paytm, PhonePe and Google Pay do UPI at a very large scale (India's UPI crossed ten billion transactions a month, confirm latest NPCI figures); one transfer is two balance changes that must be atomic.

Worked example. A has 10,000 paise, B has 0. Transfer 4,000 (key k1): A 6,000, B 4,000. Client times out and retries k1: same result returned, balances unchanged. Transfer 9,000 (key k2): FAILED, insufficient funds. Invariant: A + B = 10,000 always.

Industry examples. Stripe popularised the Idempotency-Key header: the server stores the response by key and replays it on retries. Banks use double-entry ledgers where every transfer is a debit row and a credit row summing to zero.

Everyday analogy. Moving cash between two envelopes: taking from one and not putting in the other would destroy money.

Common interview traps.

  • Using double for money. Use integer minor units (paise).
  • Forgetting idempotency; a retry double-charges.
  • Not recording failed attempts.

notes.title: Core entities
notes.html:
• Wallet: id and balance with debit and credit.
  • Tx (transaction): id, from, to, amount, status; an immutable record.
  • PaymentService: owns wallets, the ledger, and the idempotency map.
  • InsufficientFunds exception.

Decision gravity. The ledger is append-only: balances can be recomputed from it. Reversible: no, because once customers' money is involved, never rewrite history; fix with a compensating transaction.

Everyday analogy. A bank passbook: you never erase a line, you add a correcting one.

Common interview traps.

  • Updating balance without a ledger row, so you cannot audit.
  • Letting debit go negative then "fixing" later.

notes.title: Class diagram
notes.html:
+-----------------+ 1   * +----------+
| PaymentService  |------>| Wallet   |
| wallets         |       | id       |
| byKey (idem.)   |       | balance  |
| ledger          |       | debit()  |
| transfer(key,..)|       | credit() |
+-----------------+       +----------+
        | 1
        | *
+---------------------------------+
| Tx(id, from, to, amount, status)|  status: SUCCESS | FAILED
+---------------------------------+

Common interview traps.

  • Hiding the idempotency map; it is a first-class part of the design.

notes.title: Key patterns
notes.html:
• Idempotency key (not a GoF pattern, but the key idea): store result by client-supplied key; repeat returns the stored result. Alternative: dedupe by (from, to, amount, time window), which wrongly merges two real identical payments. Reversible: no, it becomes part of the API contract.
  • Command-like transaction record (Tx) as an immutable audit entry.
  • Invariant first: sum of all balances is constant across transfers. Great thing to assert in tests.
  • Not used: Strategy for fees, until fees are asked for.

Worked example. TTL of idempotency keys: Stripe keeps them about 24 hours. Choose a window longer than any client retry horizon.

Industry examples. Razorpay and Stripe both require idempotency keys on payment creation; Kafka's idempotent producer uses sequence numbers with the same goal.

Everyday analogy. A cinema ticket number: showing the same ticket twice does not admit you twice.

Common interview traps.

  • Storing the key after the money moves in a non-atomic way, so a crash in between double-charges on retry.
  • Generating the key on the server; the client must generate it.

notes.title: Code
notes.html:
import java.util.*;

enum TxStatus { SUCCESS, FAILED }
record Tx(String id, String from, String to, long amount, TxStatus status) {}

class InsufficientFunds extends RuntimeException { InsufficientFunds(String m) { super(m); } }

class Wallet {
    final String id; private long balance;               // paise, never double
    Wallet(String id, long b) { this.id = id; balance = b; }
    long balance() { return balance; }
    void debit(long amt) { if (balance < amt) throw new InsufficientFunds(id); balance -= amt; }
    void credit(long amt) { balance += amt; }
}

class PaymentService {
    private final Map<String, Wallet> wallets = new HashMap<>();
    private final Map<String, Tx> byKey = new HashMap<>();   // idempotency key -> result
    private final List<Tx> ledger = new ArrayList<>();
    private int seq = 0;

    Wallet open(String id, long initial) { Wallet w = new Wallet(id, initial); wallets.put(id, w); return w; }

    Tx transfer(String key, String from, String to, long amount) {
        Tx prev = byKey.get(key);
        if (prev != null) return prev;                       // retry-safe
        if (amount <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount");
        Wallet a = wallets.get(from), b = wallets.get(to);
        Tx tx;
        try {
            a.debit(amount); b.credit(amount);
            tx = new Tx("T" + (++seq), from, to, amount, TxStatus.SUCCESS);
        } catch (InsufficientFunds e) {
            tx = new Tx("T" + (++seq), from, to, amount, TxStatus.FAILED);
        }
        byKey.put(key, tx); ledger.add(tx);
        return tx;
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        PaymentService p = new PaymentService();
        Wallet a = p.open("a", 10_000), b = p.open("b", 0);
        System.out.println(p.transfer("k1", "a", "b", 4_000).status());
        System.out.println(p.transfer("k1", "a", "b", 4_000).status() + " (retry, not charged twice)");
        System.out.println(p.transfer("k2", "a", "b", 9_000).status());
        System.out.println(a.balance() + " " + b.balance());
        if (a.balance() + b.balance() != 10_000 || a.balance() != 6_000) throw new AssertionError();
    }
}

Kotlin core:

enum class TxStatus { SUCCESS, FAILED }
data class Tx(val id: String, val from: String, val to: String, val amount: Long, val status: TxStatus)

class Wallet(val id: String, balance: Long) {
    var balance = balance; private set
    fun debit(amt: Long) { if (balance < amt) throw IllegalStateException("insufficient"); balance -= amt }
    fun credit(amt: Long) { balance += amt }
}

class PaymentService {
    private val wallets = mutableMapOf<String, Wallet>()
    private val byKey = mutableMapOf<String, Tx>()
    private val ledger = mutableListOf<Tx>()
    private var seq = 0
    fun open(id: String, initial: Long) = Wallet(id, initial).also { wallets[id] = it }
    fun transfer(key: String, from: String, to: String, amount: Long): Tx {
        byKey[key]?.let { return it }
        require(amount > 0)
        val status = try { wallets.getValue(from).debit(amount); wallets.getValue(to).credit(amount); TxStatus.SUCCESS }
                     catch (e: IllegalStateException) { TxStatus.FAILED }
        return Tx("T${++seq}", from, to, amount, status).also { byKey[key] = it; ledger += it }
    }
}

Common interview traps.

  • Crediting the receiver before checking the debit succeeded.

notes.html:
javac -d out Main.java
java -cp out Main
SUCCESS
SUCCESS (retry, not charged twice)
FAILED
6000 4000

Test: the invariant after many random transfers, retry with the same key, amount 0 or negative, transfer to self, unknown wallet.

Common interview traps.

  • Testing only the happy path.

notes.title: Concurrency
notes.html:
This is where wallets are graded. Races: two transfers from A read balance 100 and both debit 80 (overdraft); A to B and B to A at once deadlock if each locks its source first; two threads with the same key both pass the byKey check and move money twice.

Thread-safe version. Lock both wallets in a fixed global order (by id) so two opposite transfers cannot deadlock, and make the idempotency check atomic.

class PaymentService {
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, Wallet> wallets = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, Tx> byKey = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final List<Tx> ledger = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
    private final AtomicInteger seq = new AtomicInteger();

    Tx transfer(String key, String from, String to, long amount) {
        // computeIfAbsent runs the lambda at most once per key: retries wait and get the same Tx
        return byKey.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> {
            Wallet a = wallets.get(from), b = wallets.get(to);
            Wallet first = from.compareTo(to) < 0 ? a : b;   // fixed order
            Wallet second = first == a ? b : a;
            synchronized (first) {
                synchronized (second) {
                    TxStatus st;
                    try { a.debit(amount); b.credit(amount); st = TxStatus.SUCCESS; }
                    catch (InsufficientFunds e) { st = TxStatus.FAILED; }
                    Tx tx = new Tx("T" + seq.incrementAndGet(), from, to, amount, st);
                    ledger.add(tx);
                    return tx;
                }
            }
        });
    }
}

Note the lambda touches other wallets, not byKey, so it is safe inside computeIfAbsent. Transfer to self needs a guard (from.equals(to)) because it would lock the same object twice (harmless for synchronized, a bug for non-reentrant locks).

Production note (gravity, one-way door). Across servers there are no in-JVM locks. The standard design is a database transaction: BEGIN; UPDATE wallet SET balance = balance - 4000 WHERE id='a' AND balance >= 4000; UPDATE wallet SET balance = balance + 4000 WHERE id='b'; INSERT ledger ...; INSERT idempotency (key unique) ...; COMMIT;. The unique key on idempotency makes duplicates fail atomically. Across different services or banks you cannot have one transaction, so you use a saga with compensating transfers.

Common interview traps.

  • Locking in the order of the arguments (classic deadlock).
  • Checking the balance, then debiting in a separate step.
  • Claiming distributed transactions are free.

notes.title: Follow-ups
notes.html:
• Fees and cashback: Strategy applied before debit.
  • Daily limits and fraud checks: a chain of validators (Chain of Responsibility).
  • Top-up from bank and refunds: more Tx types, saga for external steps.
  • Multi-currency: store currency with each wallet, forbid mixing without conversion.
  • Statement export and pagination of the ledger.

Common interview traps.

  • Adding a refund by deleting the original transaction.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Money as integer paise; append-only ledger; invariant: total is conserved.
  • Idempotency key stored with the result, generated by the client.
  • Thread safety: lock both wallets in a fixed order; atomic once-per-key execution.
  • In production the guarantee is a SQL transaction with conditional UPDATE and a unique idempotency key.
  • Cross-system flows are sagas, not locks.

questions.promptHtml: Why must a wallet store money as an integer number of paise (or cents) and not as a double?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A basic correctness filter for anyone touching payments.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so sums drift: 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3. Money must add up to the last unit, so I store a long count of the smallest unit (paise) and format only at the edge. If I need fractions of a paisa (interest, tax) I use BigDecimal with a stated rounding mode.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
double: 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004
long:   10 + 20   = 30    (paise)

Integer arithmetic is exact and fast, and overflow is far away: a long holds about 9.2 x 10^18 paise, i.e. 9.2 x 10^16 rupees. The invariant "total money is conserved" is only testable with exact arithmetic.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
long balance = 10_000;            // Rs 100.00
long fee = Math.round(balance * 0.015);   // percent math: choose and document rounding
var balance = 10_000L             // Rs 100.00
val fee = Math.round(balance * 0.015)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• double or float balances.
  • Mixing currencies with different minor units (JPY has none, KWD has three).
  • Rounding differently in two places so the ledger never reconciles.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What about currency conversion? -> Store a currency per wallet, forbid mixing, convert explicitly with a rate and rounding rule.
  2. Why not BigDecimal everywhere? -> Exact but slower and verbose; fine when scale varies, unnecessary for a single minor unit.
  3. Where do you format? -> At the API boundary only.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "double is inexact". Senior adds minor units per currency, rounding policy and overflow bounds.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reconciliation job found 0.01 differences per thousand transactions, all from a float in one service.

questions.promptHtml: What is an idempotency key, who generates it, and how long do you keep it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Retries are inevitable in payments; this tests whether you can make them safe.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The client generates a unique key per logical payment and sends it with every attempt. The server stores the result under that key; a repeat returns the stored result instead of moving money again. The key must be generated by the client, and stored atomically with the money movement. I keep it longer than any client retry horizon, for example 24 hours, as Stripe does.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
request(key) -> lookup key
   found -> return stored Tx   (no money moves)
   new   -> move money + store Tx under key  (ONE atomic unit)

Alternatives are weaker: dedupe by (from,to,amount,window) merges two real identical payments. If the server generated the key, a lost response gives the client nothing to retry with. If the key is stored after money moves, a crash between the two steps double-charges.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
Tx prev = byKey.get(key);
if (prev != null) return prev;                 // retry-safe
byKey[key]?.let { return it }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Key stored after the debit, non-atomically.
  • Same key reused with a different amount: should be rejected (compare a request hash), not silently replayed.
  • Server-generated keys.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Same key, different body? -> Return an error (key conflict).
  2. Two simultaneous requests with the same key? -> Unique constraint or computeIfAbsent; the second waits or gets "in progress".
  3. What does the response replay include for a failed first attempt? -> The stored FAILED result; a new key is needed to retry after fixing the cause.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE describes "dedupe by id". Senior covers atomic key-and-money storage, request fingerprint, concurrent duplicates and TTL.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Mobile clients retrying on flaky networks double-charged users until the key was made part of the API contract.

questions.contextHtml:
A refactor of transfer ships. Finance reports money appears out of nowhere: the sum of all balances grew by Rs 41,200 over a day. Failed transfers show as SUCCESS in the ledger some of the time.

Languages: Java · Kotlin
Tx transfer(String key, String from, String to, long amount) {
    Wallet a = wallets.get(from), b = wallets.get(to);
    b.credit(amount);                                  // credit first "to be safe"
    try {
        a.debit(amount);
    } catch (InsufficientFunds e) {
        ledger.add(new Tx("T" + (++seq), from, to, amount, TxStatus.FAILED));
        throw e;
    }
    Tx tx = new Tx("T" + (++seq), from, to, amount, TxStatus.SUCCESS);
    byKey.put(key, tx); ledger.add(tx);
    return tx;
}
fun transfer(key: String, from: String, to: String, amount: Long): Tx {
    val a = wallets.getValue(from); val b = wallets.getValue(to)
    b.credit(amount)                                   // credit first "to be safe"
    try { a.debit(amount) } catch (e: IllegalStateException) {
        ledger += Tx("T${++seq}", from, to, amount, TxStatus.FAILED)
        throw e
    }
    return Tx("T${++seq}", from, to, amount, TxStatus.SUCCESS).also { byKey[key] = it; ledger += it }
}
questions.promptHtml: List every defect and the corrected version.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Notices only "credit first" and swaps the order, missing idempotency, validation and self-transfer.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there a rollback mechanism? Is the call retried by clients? Can from == to?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Freeze transfers, reconcile by replaying the ledger to compute true balances, then compensate the Rs 41,200 with explicit adjustment transactions (never edit old rows).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) credit happens before the debit is known to succeed, so every insufficient-funds attempt creates money; (b) no idempotency check at the start; (c) no amount check; (d) FAILED result not stored under the key, so a retry tries again; (e) from == to.
  4. How I'd verify each: Property test: random transfers (including failing ones), assert sum of balances constant; retry with same key; negative amount.
  5. Root cause: Two balance changes are not atomic, and the failure path leaves half of them applied.
  6. Fix:
Languages: Java · Kotlin
Tx transfer(String key, String from, String to, long amount) {
    Tx prev = byKey.get(key);
    if (prev != null) return prev;
    if (amount <= 0 || from.equals(to)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad transfer");
    Wallet a = wallets.get(from), b = wallets.get(to);
    TxStatus st;
    try { a.debit(amount); b.credit(amount); st = TxStatus.SUCCESS; }   // debit first: it can fail
    catch (InsufficientFunds e) { st = TxStatus.FAILED; }
    Tx tx = new Tx("T" + (++seq), from, to, amount, st);
    byKey.put(key, tx); ledger.add(tx);
    return tx;
}
fun transfer(key: String, from: String, to: String, amount: Long): Tx {
    byKey[key]?.let { return it }
    require(amount > 0 && from != to) { "bad transfer" }
    val st = try { wallets.getValue(from).debit(amount); wallets.getValue(to).credit(amount); TxStatus.SUCCESS }
             catch (e: IllegalStateException) { TxStatus.FAILED }
    return Tx("T${++seq}", from, to, amount, st).also { byKey[key] = it; ledger += it }
}
  1. Prevention: Conservation invariant test in CI and a nightly reconciliation job comparing sum of balances with sum of ledger.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not "fix" balances by editing them; I add compensating ledger entries. In a real system this is a DB transaction, not in-memory code.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the credit throws after the debit succeeded? -> Real systems wrap both in one transaction (or compensate); in-memory the credit cannot fail.
  • Why store FAILED under the key? -> So a retry returns the same answer rather than re-running.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: "Credit first, debit later" in a payout job created duplicate money for months because the failure branch was never exercised in tests.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swaps order only.
  • Hire: also idempotency, validation, FAILED recorded.
  • Strong hire: conservation property test, reconciliation, compensating adjustments.

questions.contextHtml: Finance asks for: (1) a 1% fee on transfers above Rs 1,000 charged to the sender, (2) a daily sending limit of Rs 50,000 per wallet, (3) a promotional cashback of Rs 20 on the first transfer. Today transfer is 25 lines with no extension points.
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change and how do you structure the new rules so the next rule is cheap?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Three more ifs inside transfer, with fee maths mixed into debit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the fee part of the amount or on top? Where does the fee money go (a system wallet)? Does a failed transfer count toward the daily limit? Order of rules?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; I'd keep transfer thin: validate, price, move, record.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Options: if chain; Chain of Responsibility validators plus a Strategy for fees; a full rules engine.
  4. How I'd verify each: Which option lets me add a fourth rule without touching transfer? The chain plus strategy.
  5. Root cause: Validation (limits, balance) and pricing (fee, cashback) are different axes of change.
  6. Fix: interface Validator { void check(Transfer t); } chain (amount positive, limit, fraud later); interface FeePolicy { long fee(Transfer t); }; cashback is a second ledger entry from a system wallet (a posting), not a hidden balance tweak. Fee is a separate ledger line so the invariant still holds: sender pays amount+fee, receiver gets amount, system wallet gets fee.
  7. Prevention: Test each policy alone; conservation test with fees included; limit boundary at exactly 50,000.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No rules engine for three rules. Fee maths in integer paise with a stated rounding (round half up).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Fee changes mid-day; old transactions? -> Ledger rows are immutable and store the fee actually charged.
  • Daily limit across multiple servers? -> Counter in the DB, updated within the same transaction.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "temporary" promo tweak to balances was invisible to the ledger; reconciliation was off by the promo total until it was modelled as postings.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: inline ifs.
  • Hire: chain plus strategy.
  • Strong hire: fee and cashback as ledger entries preserving conservation, plus counter placement.

questions.contextHtml: Your wallet tests are five hand-written examples. A bug slipped through where concurrent transfers to self left a balance doubled. The team lead asks: "How do we get confidence that money is never created or destroyed?"
questions.promptHtml: Describe your test strategy for the payment service, including the concurrent case.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: More examples of the happy path, or "manual QA".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there a seedable random source? Is the service in-memory in tests or backed by a DB?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add the missing regression test (transfer to self) first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: What classes of bugs: boundary inputs, retries, failure paths, ordering/concurrency.
  4. How I'd verify each: Property-style test: seeded random sequence of 100,000 transfers (including invalid and failing), after each assert sum(balances) == initial, no balance negative, ledger replay equals balances.
  5. Root cause: Example-based tests cannot cover combinations; invariants can.
  6. Fix:
Languages: Java · Kotlin
Random rnd = new Random(42);
for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) {
    String f = "w" + rnd.nextInt(5), t = "w" + rnd.nextInt(5);
    try { svc.transfer("k" + i, f, t, rnd.nextInt(3_000)); } catch (IllegalArgumentException ignored) {}
    if (svc.total() != INITIAL_TOTAL) throw new AssertionError("seed 42, step " + i);
}
val rnd = java.util.Random(42)
repeat(100_000) { i ->
    val f = "w${rnd.nextInt(5)}"; val t = "w${rnd.nextInt(5)}"
    try { svc.transfer("k$i", f, t, rnd.nextInt(3_000).toLong()) } catch (_: IllegalArgumentException) {}
    check(svc.total() == INITIAL_TOTAL) { "seed 42, step $i" }
}

Then a concurrent version: 16 threads each doing 10,000 transfers among 5 wallets, join, assert the same invariant, plus a retry test with one key sent from 8 threads that must move money once. 7. Prevention: Print the seed on failure for reproduction; run the concurrency test in CI repeatedly; also check ledger entries count equals unique keys. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use sleep to coordinate threads; use a CountDownLatch start gate. A passing concurrent test proves little alone, so I also reason about lock order.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The test never deadlocks locally? -> Use from/to pairs that deliberately oppose each other and a timeout.
  • DB-backed? -> Same properties against a real DB in an integration test, with isolation level stated.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A seeded random test found a self-transfer double credit after 38,000 steps that no human-written example had covered.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only examples.
  • Hire: conservation invariant and retry test.
  • Strong hire: seeded reproducibility, concurrent harness, deadlock-targeted pairs.

questions.contextHtml:
After adding per-wallet locks, the service hangs a few times a day under load. Thread dump:

Found one Java-level deadlock:
"pool-3-thread-5": waiting to lock monitor 0x...a (object Wallet@7a1 [id=alice]),
                   which is held by "pool-3-thread-9"
"pool-3-thread-9": waiting to lock monitor 0x...b (object Wallet@7b2 [id=bob]),
                   which is held by "pool-3-thread-5"
Languages: Java · Kotlin
synchronized (a) {            // a = from wallet
    synchronized (b) {        // b = to wallet
        a.debit(amount); b.credit(amount);
    }
}
synchronized(a) {             // a = from wallet
    synchronized(b) {         // b = to wallet
        a.debit(amount); b.credit(amount)
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Explain the deadlock, fix it, and explain what else breaks (self-transfer, idempotency).

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a timeout" or "use tryLock and retry" without removing the cause.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Single JVM? Are wallet ids totally ordered and immutable? Do other code paths lock wallets (bulk payouts)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart is the only escape from a monitor deadlock; meanwhile route traffic away and reduce concurrency.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A to B and B to A at the same time lock in argument order: classic circular wait; (b) a third path also locks in a different order; (c) a long-held lock plus nested call into external code.
  4. How I'd verify each: jstack shows the cycle; search for every synchronized/lock() on wallets.
  5. Root cause: Circular wait: thread 1 holds alice wants bob; thread 2 holds bob wants alice.
  6. Fix: Acquire locks in a global order, e.g. by wallet id, regardless of transfer direction:
Languages: Java · Kotlin
Wallet first = from.compareTo(to) < 0 ? a : b;
Wallet second = first == a ? b : a;
synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { a.debit(amount); b.credit(amount); } }
val first = if (from < to) a else b
val second = if (first === a) b else a
synchronized(first) { synchronized(second) { a.debit(amount); b.credit(amount) } }

Reject from == to earlier. The idempotency check uses computeIfAbsent so two same-key requests run once (the lambda must not touch byKey). 7. Prevention: Stress test with opposite pairs; document the lock order in code; lint for nested locks. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: tryLock with timeout and retry avoids a hang but livelocks under contention and hides the design bug. Ordered locking removes the cycle.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Ids are not comparable (e.g. UUID strings vs numbers)? -> Any consistent total order works; System.identityHashCode ties need a tie-breaker lock.
  • Across servers? -> No JVM locks; use a DB transaction with UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= x, locking rows in id order.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A wallet service deadlocked weekly on payday when many user-to-user transfers crossed; nobody saw it in staging because traffic was one-directional.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: timeouts only.
  • Hire: ordered locking.
  • Strong hire: self-transfer, once-per-key execution, and the DB equivalent.

questions.contextHtml:
After a database failover at 02:14, support gets 340 tickets of double charges. Logs for one customer:

02:13:58 POST /transfer key=K-91 ... debit ok (txn 7741 committed)
02:13:58 idempotency store write -> ERROR connection reset
02:14:03 client retry POST /transfer key=K-91 ... key not found
02:14:03 debit ok (txn 7799 committed)

Design: step 1 UPDATE wallet, step 2 INSERT ledger, commit; step 3 separate INSERT idempotency in another transaction. Red herring: the failover itself finished cleanly in 40 s.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong, how do you remediate customers, and what is the correct design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the failover and says "make the DB highly available".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the ledger the source of truth? Do both debits reference the same client key? Can we identify duplicates now?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause retries (or rate-limit) and enable a check that rejects a second ledger row with the same client key.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) key stored in a separate transaction after the money movement, so a crash window exists; (b) ledger has no unique constraint on the key; (c) failover just widened a window that always existed.
  4. How I'd verify each: Query for ledger rows grouped by client key having count > 1.
  5. Root cause: Idempotency record and money movement are not one atomic unit, so "money moved, no record" is a reachable state.
  6. Fix: One transaction: BEGIN; INSERT idempotency(key UNIQUE) ...; UPDATE wallet SET balance = balance - :amt WHERE id=:a AND balance >= :amt; UPDATE wallet ...credit; INSERT ledger ...; COMMIT;. A duplicate key fails the whole transaction. Remediation: find duplicate groups, create compensating refund entries (never delete rows), notify customers.
SELECT idem_key, count(*) FROM ledger WHERE created_at >= '2026-11-13 02:00' GROUP BY idem_key HAVING count(*) > 1;
  1. Prevention: Unique constraint on the key in the ledger itself; chaos test that kills the connection between steps; reconciliation job.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use a time-window dedupe heuristic (it would merge real identical payments). I would not delete the duplicate rows.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Key store in Redis, money in SQL? -> Cannot be atomic; you then need the SQL unique key as the authority and Redis only as a fast path.
  • Response lost but transaction committed? -> Retry hits the unique key and returns the stored result.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A payments team had an "in progress" marker written before and a "done" marker after; crash recovery used the markers to resolve ambiguous transfers exactly once.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames infrastructure.
  • Hire: puts key in the same transaction with a unique constraint.
  • Strong hire: remediation with compensating entries, detection query, chaos test.

questions.contextHtml: A new "withdraw to bank" feature: debit the wallet, call the bank API (200-3,000 ms, sometimes times out), then mark done. Bank timeouts happen on 0.5% of calls; in those cases the bank may or may not have executed the transfer. A teammate proposes holding a DB transaction open across the bank call "to keep it atomic".
questions.promptHtml: Design the flow and handle the ambiguous timeout.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Holds the DB transaction across the HTTP call, or refunds immediately on any exception.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the bank API support idempotency keys and a status query? Settlement time? Reconciliation file from the bank?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; I'd state the principle: no distributed transaction, use a saga with persisted state.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Options: (a) DB transaction around the call (locks held for seconds, still no atomicity with the bank); (b) refund on error (double payout if the bank did execute); (c) saga: reserve funds, call bank with our key, resolve via status.
  4. How I'd verify each: Failure matrix: crash before call, after call, timeout, bank says failed.
  5. Root cause: The bank is a separate system; two systems cannot share a transaction.
  6. Fix: Saga with states RESERVED -> SUBMITTED -> CONFIRMED | FAILED | UNKNOWN. Step 1: transaction moves funds to a hold and writes state RESERVED with a key. Step 2: call bank with the same key. Timeout moves to UNKNOWN, never to refund. A resolver polls the bank's status (or reconciliation file) and then either confirms or refunds with a compensating ledger entry.
  7. Prevention: State machine tests with fault injection at each step; alert on transactions stuck in UNKNOWN longer than a threshold.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not auto-refund on timeout. The cost is delayed funds for 0.5% of users; the benefit is never paying out twice.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Bank has no idempotency support? -> Then retries are dangerous; rely on status queries or reconciliation before any retry, and escalate to manual review.
  • Process crashes after the bank call? -> On restart the resolver finds SUBMITTED rows and queries the bank.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A refund-on-error payout flow paid users twice whenever the bank was slow but successful; a persisted UNKNOWN state fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: long transaction or blind refund.
  • Hire: saga with persisted state.
  • Strong hire: UNKNOWN state, status polling or reconciliation, never auto-refund on timeout.
